title.en: Hanan and Hurin Cuzco: The Two Branches of the Inca Lineage
title.zh: 哈南與烏林庫斯科:印加王族的兩支

region.zh: 庫斯科谷地(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The lineage of these Yncas was divided into two branches, the one called Hanan Cuzco and the other Hurin Cuzco. From this it may be concluded that they were natives of the valley of Cuzco, although some pretend that they came from other parts to settle there - but no credit should be given to them, for they also say that this happened before the flood. From the traditions of the present time it is not more than three hundred and fifty to four hundred years since the Yncas only possessed and ruled over the valley of Cuzco as far as Urcos and the valley of Yucay. They preserve the memory of these Lords by their quipus; but, judged by the time each is said to have lived, the historical period cannot be placed further back than four hundred years at the earliest.
summary.zh: 印加王族分為兩支:一稱「哈南庫斯科」(上庫斯科),一稱「烏林庫斯科」(下庫斯科)。由此可斷:他們本是庫斯科谷地的土著;雖有人稱其自他處遷來——但此說不足信,因那些人還說遷來之事發生在洪水之前。就現存傳說推算,印加人僅據庫斯科谷地——東至烏爾科斯、北至尤卡伊谷——不過三百五十年至四百年。諸王之名以結繩「基普」記憶;但按諸王在位年數推算,信史至多上溯四百年。

sensitivity.note: Polo's source-critical frame: the Hanan/Hurin duality as the oldest social fact of Cuzco; his skepticism about pre-flood origins is quoted.

passages.text: It must be understood, in the first place, that the lineage of these Yncas was divided into two branches, the one called Hanan Cuzco, and the other Hurin Cuzco. From this it may be concluded (and there is no memory of anything to the contrary) that they were natives of the valley of Cuzco, although some pretend that they came from other parts to settle there. But no credit should be given to them, for they also say that this happened before the flood.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: From what can be gathered and conjectured in considering the traditions of the present time, it is not more than three hundred and fifty to four hundred years since the Yncas only possessed and ruled over the valley of Cuzco as far as Urcos, a distance of six leagues, and to the valley of Yucay, which is not more than five leagues. They preserve the memory of these Lords by their quipus, but if we judge by the time that each is said to have lived, the historical period cannot be placed further back than four hundred years at the earliest.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Pururaucas: Seven from the Cave and Warriors Sent from Heaven
title.zh: 普魯勞卡斯:洞中七人與天降援兵

region.en: Paccari-tampu, five leagues from Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近帕卡里坦波(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Having resolved to conquer and subjugate other nations, the Yncas sought some colour and pretext for prosecuting their objects. The first story they put forward was that, after the deluge, seven men and women had come out of a cave which they call Paccari-tampu, five leagues from Cuzco, where a window was carved in masonry in most ancient times; that these persons multiplied and spread over the world - hence every province had a like place of worship where people came forth after the universal destruction. His father having been defeated by the Chancas, Pachacuti formed an army from the fugitives, the garrison of Cuzco and the men of Canes and Canches; before he set out his mother had a dream that the reason of the Chanca victory was that more veneration was shown for the Sun than for Pachayachachic, the universal Creator. Henceforward a promise was made that more sacrifices and prayers should be offered to that statue; then the son was promised a victory over the Chancas, and that men should be sent from Heaven to reinforce him. With this title he went forth and conquered, and thence arose the idea of the Pururaucas - the stone allies - most important for the Yncas as a title in extending their conquests. All who were subjugated were taught that Cuzco was the abode and home of the gods; throughout that city there was not a fountain, nor a well, nor a wall, which they did not say contained some mystery - more than four hundred such places of worship are enumerated in the report on Cuzco.
summary.zh: 印加人決意征服他邦,便需尋一藉口。最初提出的說法是:洪水之後,七位男女自庫斯科附近(五萊格)一處名「帕卡里坦波」的洞穴走出——那裡的古牆上鑿有一窗;此七人繁衍子孫,遍布天下——故各省皆有同類聖地,相傳大毀滅後人們皆從那裡走出。帕查庫提之父為昌卡人所敗,退保庫斯科;帕查庫提以潰卒、城防軍與卡內斯、坎切斯人重組大軍。出征之前,其母得一夢:昌卡人獲勝,是因世人崇太陽過於崇「帕查亞查奇」——造化萬物之主。自此立誓,對造物主之像多獻祭多祈禱;隨後有人許諾:其子必勝昌卡,且天將遣神兵相助。他持此「天命」出征而克,遂生「普魯勞卡斯」之說——化石為兵者——成為印加擴張最重要的名義。凡被征服者皆受教:庫斯科是諸神的居所;全城之內,無一泉、一井、一牆不含神異——庫斯科聖所清單所載,不下四百處。

sensitivity.note: Polo's uniquely candid analysis of Inca conquest ideology as manufactured title; the Pururaucas (petrified allies) are the political theology of the Chanca war.

passages.text: Having resolved to conquer and subjugate other nations, the Yncas sought some colour and pretext for prosecuting their objects. The first story that these Yncas put forward, though it was not the title which they finally asserted, was an idea that, after the deluge, seven men and women had come out of a cave which they call Paccari-tampu, five leagues from Cuzco, where a window was carved in masonry in most ancient times; that these persons multiplied and spread over the world. Hence every province had a like place of worship where people came forth after the universal destruction.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: His father had been defeated by the Chancas, and retreated to Cuzco, leaving his troops in a Pucara or fortress. Then the son formed an army out of the fugitives, and out of the garrison of Cuzco, and out of the men of Canes and Canches, and turned back to attack the Chancas. Before he set out his mother had a dream that the reason of the victory of the Chancas was that more veneration was shown for the Sun than Pachayachachic, who was the universal Creator. Henceforward a promise was made that more sacrifices and prayers should be offered to that statue. Then the son was promised a victory over the Chancas, and that men should be sent from Heaven to reinforce him. With this title he went forth and conquered, and thence arose that idea of the Pururaucas, which was one which was most important for the Yncas as a title in extending their conquests.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sacrifices of many kinds were continually invented, and all who were subjugated were taught that Cuzco was the abode and home of the gods. Throughout that city there was not a fountain, nor a well, nor a wall, which they did not say contained some mystery, as appears in the report on the places of worship in that city, where more than four hundred such places are enumerated.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lands of the Sun and of the Inca: Singing Work-Parties
title.zh: 太陽之田與印加之田:歌聲中的勞作

region.zh: 大蘇尤各村田地(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In every place where a settlement was formed, the land was divided as follows: one portion was set apart for the support of religion, being divided between the Sun and the Pachayachachic, and the thunder which they called Chuquilla, and the Pacha-mama and their ministers, and other huacas and places of worship. Every notable thing was made an object of worship - springs, fountains, streams, stones, valleys, and hill summits, which they called apachetas - each with its people whose duty it was to perform the sacrifices. The lands of the tribute of the Ynca and of religion were sown and reaped in the same order; when the people worked upon them they ate and drank at the cost of the Ynca and of the Sun. This work was not performed by gangs: all the inhabitants went forth except the aged and infirm, dressed in their best clothes, and singing songs appropriate for the occasion. Although the crops were devoted to the tribute, the land itself belonged to the people themselves; the aged, infirm, and widows did not join in the work.
summary.zh: 凡立村之處,土地如此分配:一份供養宗教——分歸太陽、帕查亞查奇、名喚「楚基利亞」的雷神、帕查-瑪瑪(地母)及其祭司,以及其他瓦卡與聖所。凡可注目之物皆成崇拜對象——泉、井、溪流、石、谷、峰頂(所謂「阿帕凱塔斯」)——各配專司祭祀之人。印加與宗教的貢田,播種收穫皆依同例;勞作之時,飲食皆由印加與太陽供給。此勞非按隊攤派:除老弱之外,全體居民盛裝而出,唱著應時的歌謠下田。雖收穫盡歲貢,土地本身仍屬人民;老弱與寡婦不與此役。

sensitivity.note: Polo's administrative description of the religious economy; the singing-work detail is a rare social texture.

passages.text: In every place where a settlement or village community was formed, the land was divided in the following manner: one portion was set apart for the support of religion, being divided between the Sun and the Pachayachachic, and the thunder, which they called Chuquilla, and the Pacha-mama and their ministers, and other huacas and places of worship. For each town was divided in the same way as Cuzco, and every notable thing was made an object of worship, such as springs, fountains, streams, stones, valleys, and hill summits, which they called apachetas. Each of these things had its people whose duty it was to perform the sacrifices.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lands set apart for the tribute of the Ynca and of religion were sown and reaped in the same order; but it must be understood that when the people worked upon them, they ate and drank at the cost of the Ynca and of the Sun. This work was not performed by gangs, nor were the men told off for it, but all the inhabitants went forth except the aged and infirm, dressed in their best clothes, and singing songs appropriate for the occasion. In these two kinds of tribute there were two things that seem worthy of note: one is that the aged, infirm, and widows did not join in it; the other is, that although the crops and other produce of these lands were devoted to the tribute, the land itself belonged to the people themselves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Ccapac-llama and Huachay-llama: The Flocks of the Rich and the Poor
title.zh: 卡帕克-利亞馬與瓜恰伊-利亞馬:富畜與貧畜

region.en: High pastures of the Collao (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞奧高原牧場(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Those flocks belonging to religion and to the Ynca were called Ccapac-llama, and the others Huachay-llama, which means rich and poor beasts. A division was prohibited, and to this day they are all enjoyed in common. There was a rule that females should never be killed, and thus the flocks multiplied exceedingly, for neither were those of the Ynca or of religion killed except for sacrifices. If any beast was attacked with carache, the disease by which so many have been lost in our times, the rule was that they should not be fed or cured, but buried at once, deep in the ground, as the disease was infectious. The flock of the community was shorn at the proper season, and the wool was divided amongst the people, each getting the quantity he required for himself, his wife, and children; so that all were clothed.
summary.zh: 歸宗教與印加所有的畜群稱「卡帕克-利亞馬」,其餘稱「瓜恰伊-利亞馬」——意即「富畜」與「貧畜」。此種劃分不許取消,至今全民共用。律有一條:母畜永不得宰殺——故畜群繁殖極盛;印加與宗教的畜群,除祭祀外亦不輕宰。若有牲畜染上「卡拉切」疫病(近世因此損失甚眾),律令不得餵養醫治,須立即深埋土中,以防傳染。村中公畜按時剪毛,羊毛按人分配——本人、妻、子各得所需——故人人有衣。

sensitivity.note: Pastoral law with a ritual naming; the no-female-slaughter rule framed as taboo.

title.en: No Sowing, No Share: The Ayllu's Common Harvest Rule
title.zh: 不耕者不得食:世系公田之分穀律

region.zh: 庫斯科地區(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: On the death of an owner of land, the heirs and descendants possessed it in common, without the power of dividing it; but the person who represented the Ayllu had the charge, and all the rest enjoyed the fruits in common, divided among them as follows: if a son of the first possessor had six sons, and another son had two, each one had equal shares, and there were as many shares as persons. At the time of sowing they all had to be present to divide the crop; and at the harvest if any one, even though a descendant, had not been at the sowing, he could neither take his share nor give it to another. Yet even if he was absent ten years, he did not lose his right, if he chose to be at the sowing; and even when there were so many descendants that there was scarcely a mazorca of maize for each, the rule was still observed; and it is still kept up in the district of Cuzco. Thus the lands belonged to the whole village, and he who did not work at the sowing had no share in the harvest.
summary.zh: 田主身故,其子孫共同擁有田地,不得分拆;由代表世系「阿伊柳」者掌其事,眾人共享其利,分配之法如下:長子若生六子、次子若生二子,則八人均分——人各一份,不以房支為限。播種之時,人人須到場分穀;收穫之際,凡未參與播種者——即便是嫡系子孫——既不得取其份,亦不得轉讓他人。然而縱使缺席十年,只要播種之日願來,其權不滅;乃至子孫繁衍到每人幾乎分不到一根玉米穗,此律依然奉行——今日庫斯科地區猶遵行之。故田屬全村:不播者,不得收。

sensitivity.note: Andean land-tenure custom described by the colonial judge; a social ethic ('no sowing, no share') rather than myth strictly - tagged ritual-origin as a customary-law story.
